text: The rice stem (culm) consists of alternating nodes (solid joints, each capable of producing a leaf and, at lower nodes, a tiller) and internodes (the hollow segments between nodes). Internodes elongate progressively less toward the base of the plant and more toward the top, meaning the lowest internodes stay short/compressed while upper internodes elongate more as the plant approaches heading. Tillering - the production of additional stems from the base of the main stem - is described using a numbering system from a classic study (Katayama, 1951): the main stem is called T0; tillers that emerge directly from the main stem are primary tillers, numbered T1, T2, T3, etc. in order of emergence; tillers that emerge from a primary tiller are secondary tillers (e.g. a tiller emerging from T1 would be numbered T11, T12, etc.); and tillers emerging from secondary tillers are tertiary tillers (numbered accordingly, e.g. T111, T121). This numbering convention lets researchers track exactly which tiller produced which subsequent tiller. Later-emerging tillers generally have less time to develop before harvest and so tend to produce smaller panicles or, if too late, may not produce a panicle at all - the number of productive tillers per plant is one of the main components of final yield.
caveat: This is detailed anatomical/developmental reference content that likely overlaps with any existing general 'plant morphology' or 'growth stages' entry in the knowledge base - recommend a duplicate-check once repo access is available. The Katayama tiller-numbering convention (T0, T1, T11, etc.) may be a useful addition if not already present, since it gives a precise way to describe tiller order that farmer-facing content sometimes needs when discussing tillering management.
